name: Foam roller

lead: A foam roller is a dense foam cylinder you roll your body weight across for self-massage. Placed under the upper back, it is also used for thoracic extension, a popular drill for people who sit for long periods and want a less rounded posture.

Pressure on the tissue is thought to reduce perceived stiffness through neural and sensory effects. A multilevel meta-analysis of 26 trials found foam rolling increases joint range of motion acutely, and a 2022 meta-analysis found no significant difference from stretching. Studies of training effects over weeks report small changes in range of motion, and no trial tests whether thoracic rolling changes resting posture.

paras: People roll before or after training, or in desk-break routines, working through muscle groups and lying lengthwise or crosswise under the upper back. It is often combined with stretching and strengthening for the back and shoulders.
Aggressive rolling can cause bruising and soreness, and rolling over the lower back, joints or neck is discouraged. Mobility effects are short-lived.

angle.text: Rolling loosens tight muscles and lets you extend the upper back, which can make you feel less hunched after long sitting and recover faster between sessions. Meta-analyses show short-term range-of-motion gains; lasting posture change is reported by users rather than tested.

lead: A foam roller is a cylinder of dense foam, commonly 30 to 90 cm long and 12 to 15 cm in diameter, on which a person rolls their body weight over muscle groups as a form of self-massage, often called self-myofascial release.[1][2] People use it before or after training to loosen tight areas, and in posture-oriented routines it is also placed under the upper back for thoracic extension drills, a favourite of people who sit for long periods and want a more upright, open-chested carriage.

For looks, the roller works through a chain: loosened and more mobile muscles and joints allow easier access to full-range positions, which supports posture work and training quality, and less perceived soreness can mean more consistent training and therefore more muscle over time. Posture communities add that an upright frame with open shoulders reads as taller and broader.

A large research literature examines foam rolling. Meta-analyses report that rolling increases joint range of motion acutely, that effects on performance are small, and that its range-of-motion effect is comparable to stretching.[3][4][5][6] Studies of training effects over weeks report small changes in range of motion.[5] Findings on soreness and recovery are mixed, and no trial cited here has tested whether thoracic-extension rolling changes resting posture over the long term.
infobox: Smooth, textured or grid surfaces; vibrating rollers; roller sticks[7]
About 90 seconds per muscle group (review recommendation)[15][2]
Associated with the Feldenkrais Method; adapted for self-massage in 1987[1]

paras: Rollers are made from foam, commonly EVA or similar elastomers, in varying densities. Wikipedia describes the tool as a lightweight cylindrical tube of elastomeric foam placed between the muscle and the floor so that body weight supplies the pressure, and notes that rollers differ in size and firmness, with softer ones suggested for beginners.[2] Surfaces may be smooth or have ridges and grids intended to deliver more focused pressure. A Grokipedia article lists typical dimensions of 12 to 36 inches in length and 5 to 6 inches in diameter.[1]

Related tools include roller sticks, massage balls and, more recently, vibrating foam rollers.[7] Laboratory work has compared how different roller designs load soft tissue: a 2008 study measured the pressure exerted on soft tissue by two types of myofascial roller.[8] Foam-roller-based exercise has also been built into programmes for older adults, with a 2024 trial examining functional fitness, balance and gait in older women.[9]

Foam rolling is a self-applied form of myofascial release, an umbrella term for massage-like manual techniques aimed at fascia, the connective tissue that wraps muscle. According to Wikipedia's myofascial release article, osteopathy's founder Andrew Taylor Still and his early students promoted fascia-focused approaches, the term itself is reported to have been coined in the 1960s by the osteopath Robert Ward, who had studied with Ida Rolf, and the therapist John F. Barnes popularised it through seminars and a 1990 book.[10]

A Grokipedia account traces the roller to the Feldenkrais Method, the somatic-education approach founded by Moshe Feldenkrais, in which foam cylinders were used as supports in movement lessons. The same article says the physical therapist Sean Gallagher, who had trained as a Feldenkrais practitioner, adapted rollers for clinical self-massage in 1987, and that Mike Clark helped bring them into athletic training in the 1990s.[1] It also states that the American College of Sports Medicine ranked foam rolling the fourteenth global fitness trend of 2019.[1] These details come from an AI-generated source and its dates are not entirely consistent, so they are given as that source's account.

By the 2010s the roller had moved from physical-therapy clinics into commercial gyms, home fitness and online mobility content, and researchers began publishing controlled trials in sports-medicine journals. Landmark early studies include a 2013 laboratory study of 11 active men on range of motion and force,[11] and 2014 studies on recovery after intense exercise[12] and on the effect of rolling versus static stretching on passive hip-flexion range of motion.[13]

Rolling applies sustained pressure, generated by body weight, to the soft tissue. The older explanation, that rolling breaks up fascial adhesions or knots, has been questioned. The Grokipedia summary describes limited evidence for mechanical changes in tissue stiffness and favours explanations based on the nervous system, such as increased stretch tolerance and pain modulation through mechanoreceptor input (gate-control theory), plus possible parasympathetic effects, and adds that precise mechanisms are still under investigation.[1]

Proponents of myofascial release more broadly say that it relaxes contracted muscle, improves circulation and stimulates the stretch reflex, while the American Cancer Society, quoted in Wikipedia's article, says there is little scientific evidence for claims that myofascial release relieves pain or restores flexibility.[10] A 2014 study examined the acute effect of rolling on arterial function,[14] reflecting interest in effects beyond the muscle itself.

People commonly roll for a short time per muscle group before training as a warm-up or afterwards as a cool-down. A 2019 review noted by Wikipedia found that about 90 seconds of rolling per muscle group may be the minimum for a short-term reduction in soreness, with insufficient evidence for an optimal duration, and a 2023 systematic review likewise suggested at least 90 seconds per muscle group.[15][2] A 2015 study examined how rolling duration affects hamstring range of motion.[16] Wikipedia reports that combining rolling with stretching changes range of motion little compared with either alone, with stretching after rolling having a significant but trivial advantage over stretching alone.[2]

Popular areas include the quadriceps, hamstrings, calves, glutes, iliotibial band and upper back. Posture-focused routines lie across the roller lengthwise or crosswise under the upper back and extend over it. Forum members also describe rolling the hip flexors, and T Nation threads link to videos of psoas releases and of squeezing a roller between the knees to work the adductors.[17][18]

A systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis in Sports Medicine in 2020 pooled trials of acute foam rolling and reported increases in joint range of motion in healthy adults.[3] A 2022 meta-analysis of training effects over weeks found small improvements in range of motion.[5] A 2022 trial in the European Journal of Applied Physiology compared a single bout of stretching with foam rolling in healthy adults.[4] A 2013 laboratory study of 11 active men reported that an acute bout of self-myofascial release increased knee range of motion without a subsequent decrease in muscle activation or force.[11]

Randomised trials have compared foam rolling with proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation stretching for hamstring flexibility in amateur athletes,[19] examined muscle flexibility in recreational long-distance runners,[20] and compared different myofascial techniques in athletes with iliotibial band tightness.[21] A 2024 randomised trial varied rolling speed and measured quadriceps mechanical properties,[22] and a 2022 trial compared high- and low-frequency vibration rolling on the quadriceps.[23]

A 2019 meta-analysis of 21 studies in Frontiers in Physiology reported that rolling before exercise produced a small improvement in sprint performance (about 0.7 per cent, g = 0.28), among other findings, and also covered rolling used after exercise as a recovery strategy.[24] A 2015 systematic review in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy appraised foam rolls and roller massagers for range of motion, post-exercise muscle recovery and performance,[6] and a 2015 literature review asked whether self-myofascial release is an effective pre-exercise and recovery strategy.[25] A 2014 randomised study of 20 trained men tested rolling as a recovery tool after an intense bout of exercise, with soreness, range of motion and vertical jump among its outcomes.[12] A 2021 trial compared several strategies for recovery after eccentric exercise-induced fatigue.[26]

A 2023 meta-analysis of five studies with 151 participants found no significant between-group difference between foam roller or stick massage and non-intervention after muscle-damaging exercise on the markers analysed, with studies at moderate to high risk of bias.[27] A 2022 meta-analysis of vibrating foam rollers, including 9 studies, found no significant effect on jump performance (SMD 0.14).[7] A 2023 systematic review of ten randomised trials reported that rolling was relevant for countermovement jump performance and that it increases flexibility without improving aerobic activity.[15] Wikipedia summarises one meta-analysis as supporting rolling as a warm-up activity more than as a recovery tool, while noting that post-exercise rolling reduced perceived muscle pain.[2]

Thoracic extension rolling is a widely shared routine in posture communities. The trials above mostly examine limb muscles and athletic outcomes. A 2017 randomised trial examined whether foam-roller exercises have a short-term effect on the thoracolumbar fascia,[28] and a 2019 randomised trial examined the training effects of foam rolling on core strength endurance, balance, performance and range of motion.[29] No study cited here has tested whether using a roller under the upper back changes resting spinal alignment over the long term.
A 2023 review of physiotherapy for plantar fasciitis lists foam roller stretching among interventions that were associated with reduced pain and improved foot function in the included studies.[30]

The Grokipedia summary describes foam rolling as generally safe but advises avoiding direct pressure on bones, joints and injured areas, and consulting a health-care provider in conditions such as acute tears, pregnancy or chronic conditions.[1] Rolling firmly can leave bruising or soreness. Guidance from clinicians commonly cautions against rolling over the lower back and neck, where the spine is not shielded by large muscle masses.

Regulators have also looked at claims made for myofascial release as a service: in 2011 the UK Advertising Standards Authority upheld a complaint against a myofascial release company, ruling that the evidence did not establish a robust body of scientific support for its claims.[10]

In posture and mobility sections of appearance communities, the roller is typically described as a way to open a rounded upper back and loosen tight areas before exercises that target the muscles between and below the shoulder blades. Proponents describe a feeling of more upright posture and loosened muscles after a session, and tie that to a taller, broader-shouldered look. Lifters on strength forums mention the roller as a self-treatment tool for hip and groin tightness,[17][18] and one poster joked that a roller works as an in-house chiropractor.[31]

Research summarised above supports short-term increases in range of motion, and effects that last are described as small. Practices adjacent to rolling in these circles include stretching, mobility drills, wall and floor posture exercises, and massage balls.

Related practices include static and PNF stretching, massage-gun percussion, massage balls and sticks, instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilisation, and manual myofascial release by a therapist.[15][10]

lore.intro: Foam rolling appears in posture, mobility and training threads as a way to loosen tight muscles, open a rounded upper back and recover between sessions, and is often paired with stretching and strengthening exercises.[17][18][31]

claims.claim: Rolling breaks up knots and adhesions in the fascia.
Foam rolling increases flexibility and range of motion.
Rolling the upper back over a roller fixes rounded-shoulder posture.
Rolling speeds recovery and reduces soreness.
A roller can stand in for a physio or chiropractor.
Harder, spikier or vibrating rollers work better.

timeline.event: The term myofascial release is reported to be coined by osteopath Robert Ward, who had studied with Ida Rolf.[10]
Physical therapist Sean Gallagher is reported to have adapted foam rollers for clinical self-massage.[1]
John F. Barnes publishes Myofascial Release: The Search for Excellence, helping popularise the approach.[10]
Mike Clark is reported to have brought rollers into athletic training.[1]
A laboratory study compares the pressure exerted on soft tissue by two types of myofascial roller.[8]
The UK Advertising Standards Authority upholds a complaint about a myofascial release company's evidence claims.[10]
A laboratory study reports increased range of motion after self-myofascial release without a subsequent decrease in activation or force.[11]
A systematic review in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy appraises rolling for range of motion, recovery and performance.[6]
A meta-analysis of foam rolling on performance and recovery is published; the American College of Sports Medicine ranks foam rolling a top fitness trend, per Grokipedia.[1][24]
A multilevel meta-analysis reports acute range-of-motion increases from foam rolling.[3]
Meta-analyses examine foam-rolling training effects and vibrating rollers.[5][7]

A meta-analysis finds no significant difference from no intervention on muscle-damage markers after exercise, and a systematic review compares foam rolling with instrument-assisted mobilisation.[27][15]
